title: Exxon Mobil XOM stock: Q1 beat and key dividend update - Rolling Out
content: ExxonMobil is drawing attention on two fronts at once. Shares of the energy giant moved higher today after the company returned to drilling in Guyana’s Canje block, while a recently reported first-quarter earnings beat and an upcoming dividend payout are keeping income-focused investors closely engaged with one of the world’s most widely held energy stocks. Shares of ExxonMobil were trading around $158 today, up modestly during the session. The stock has advanced more than 40% from its 52-week low of $101.18 but remains below its 52-week high of $176.41. ExxonMobil released its first-quarter 2026 results on May 1, posting earnings per share of $1.16 against a consensus estimate of $0.98. Revenue of $83.16 billion also topped analyst expectations of $81.13 billion. Return on equity came in at 10.24% and net margin at 7.57%. Despite the headline performance, the company registered its lowest net income in five years during the quarter. The culprit was global supply disruption tied to the Middle East conflict. ExxonMobil noted that roughly 15% of its worldwide output is currently affected by the situation, and projected that if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed through the second quarter, daily production could drop by approximately 750,000 barrels. Total global output reached 4.59 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in the quarter, a slight gain year over year but around 8% below the prior quarter’s 5 million barrels per day. Production gains in Guyana and the Permian Basin were meaningful contributors to the quarter’s performance. The company has outlined plans to grow Permian output to 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels by 2026. The return to activity in the Canje block placed ExxonMobil’s Guyana strategy back in focus for traders and analysts. Guyana has emerged as one of the most important offshore energy regions in the world, and resumed exploration there adds a near-term milestone for investors tracking the company’s upstream growth path. Progress in the Canje block would reinforce the company’s ability to extend its production runway while managing the uncertainty surrounding output from the Middle East. ExxonMobil went ex-dividend on May 15, ahead of a cash payment of $1.03 per share scheduled for June 10. The quarterly payout continues the company’s long track record of regular distributions, but the strong share price rally of the past year has compressed the dividend yield to roughly 2.61%, its lowest point in more than a decade. The dividend currently accounts for about 68% of earnings, a manageable ratio for a mature energy company, but represents approximately 92% of free cash flow, leaving a relatively narrow cushion if energy market conditions soften or capital spending accelerates. UBS maintained a Buy rating and raised its ExxonMobil price target to $174 from $171, expressing confidence in the company’s strategic positioning and citing its Guyana and Permian assets as buffers against production headwinds from geopolitical pressures elsewhere. UBS’s revised target implies upside of more than 10% from current levels. The stock carries a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 26.68, with a forward ratio of 13.71 reflecting analyst expectations for profitability as energy market conditions normalize. title: Exxon Mobil Corp. stock (US30231G1022): dividend milestone and Q1 beat keep focus on cash flows - AD HOC NEWS
content: Exxon Mobil Corp. has gone ex-dividend with a June payout ahead and recently reported Q1 2026 earnings that beat forecasts, while a strong share price rally tightens the coverage of its dividend by free cash flow. Exxon Mobil Corp. is back in focus for energy and income investors after the US oil and gas major went ex-dividend on May 15, 2026, ahead of a planned cash payout of 1.03 USD per share on June 10, 2026, according to a dividend-focused update from DripInvesting as of 05/16/2026. At the same time, the company’s Q1 2026 results released on May 1, 2026, showed earnings per share of 1.16 USD on revenue of 83.16 billion USD, topping consensus estimates of 0.98 USD EPS and 81.13 billion USD revenue, as summarized by MarketBeat as of 05/15/2026. By the editorial team – specialized in equity coverage. Exxon Mobil Corp. is one of the largest integrated energy companies worldwide, active across the full oil and gas value chain. The group explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas, refines crude into fuels and lubricants, and manufactures a broad range of petrochemical products used in plastics and industrial applications. Its size, asset base and global reach give it a central role in the energy supply chain for US and international customers. The company’s integrated structure is designed to balance earnings across commodity cycles. Upstream operations benefit from higher oil and gas prices, while downstream and chemicals can provide support when upstream margins come under pressure. This model was visible in past periods where the combination of production volumes and refining margins shaped overall profitability, as reflected in analyses of Exxon Mobil’s segment performance during prior years, such as the noted strength in upstream revenue growth in 2025 discussed by Kavout in an article dated 04/10/2025, according to Kavout as of 04/10/2025. From a financial perspective, Exxon Mobil has generated substantial net income and cash flows in recent years. Over the last four reported quarters the company delivered earnings per share of 5.93 USD, with a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 26.60 based on recent prices, while the forward price-to-earnings ratio stood at 13.71, according to MarketBeat’s earnings overview as of 05/15/2026. The stock traded near 157.72 USD at the close on May 15, 2026, on the New York Stock Exchange, implying a market value in the mid-hundreds of billions of dollars, as cited by MarketBeat as of 05/15/2026. For US investors, Exxon Mobil represents both a large-cap energy exposure and a key component of major US equity benchmarks. Its performance tends to be closely linked to global energy prices, refining margins and chemicals demand, making the stock a barometer for broader energy market trends. In addition, the company’s long history of dividend payments and capital returns has made it a reference point for income-focused portfolios, even as the energy transition and decarbonization policies continue to shape long-term strategic decisions. Exxon Mobil’s revenue base is primarily driven by its upstream segment, which encompasses the exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas. Higher commodity prices and increased production volumes can significantly lift segment earnings, while lower prices or operational disruptions can compress margins. Past analyses have highlighted that upstream revenue can react strongly to price movements, with one research article observing a 41% increase in upstream revenue and a 234% jump in US upstream operations in Q1 2025 as prices rose, according to Kavout as of 04/10/2025. Downstream operations, which include refining crude oil into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, are another important profit contributor. These activities benefit from favorable crack spreads, which measure the difference between refined product prices and crude feedstock costs. When refining margins are robust, they can partially offset weakness in upstream results. Petrochemical production, including olefins, aromatics and polymers, adds a further earnings pillar that is sensitive to global industrial activity and end-market demand, such as packaging, automotive and construction. In Q1 2026, Exxon Mobil reported revenue of 83.16 billion USD and earnings per share of 1.16 USD, surpassing consensus expectations of 81.13 billion USD in revenue and 0.98 USD in EPS, according to MarketBeat’s earnings summary as of 05/15/2026. The company posted a return on equity of 10.24% and a net margin of 7.57% for the quarter, reflecting solid profitability for a mature integrated energy group, as detailed by MarketBeat as of 05/18/2026. These metrics underline the importance of operational efficiency and disciplined capital allocation in sustaining earnings. Beyond traditional hydrocarbons, Exxon Mobil has been investing in lower-carbon initiatives, including carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, and biofuels, though these activities currently represent a smaller share of revenue compared with oil, gas and chemicals. For now, the company’s financial results remain primarily tied to the performance of its legacy energy businesses, but the scale and timing of transition-related investments could influence future growth and risk profiles. Investors tracking the stock often monitor both the progress of these projects and how they interact with regulatory developments in the United States and other key markets. The recent ex-dividend date on May 15, 2026, has drawn attention to Exxon Mobil’s capital return policy. According to a dividend-focused article from DripInvesting dated 05/16/2026, shareholders of record before the ex-dividend will receive a quarterly dividend of 1.03 USD per share on June 10, 2026. This payment continues the company’s pattern of regular distributions and underscores its emphasis on returning cash to shareholders, as highlighted by DripInvesting as of 05/16/2026. However, the same analysis notes that rising share prices have compressed the dividend yield to around 2.7%, which is described as the lowest level in more than ten years. The article indicates that the dividend consumes roughly 68% of earnings, a payout ratio commonly regarded as manageable for a mature and cash-generating company. At the same time, free cash flow coverage appears tighter, with dividends representing about 92% of free cash flow in the period under review. That means only a relatively small buffer remains if free cash flow were to decline due to weaker energy prices or higher capital spending, according to DripInvesting as of 05/16/2026. For income-oriented investors, this balance between earnings, cash flow and capital returns is a central consideration. Exxon's history of maintaining and gradually growing its dividend is a key part of its equity story, particularly in US markets where many institutional and retail investors view the company as a core dividend holding. Nonetheless, the gap between earnings-based coverage and free cash flow coverage raises questions about how resilient the payout would be if macro conditions turn less favorable, or if the company accelerates spending on large-scale projects and energy transition investments. The interaction of dividends and share buybacks also plays a role. title: Exxon Mobil (XOM): Rallies as Crude Prices Top $109 and Investor Lawsuit Risk Clears - parameter.io
content: Exxon Mobil shares ended Friday on a strong note, extending a steady weekly climb as crude oil prices surged to multi-month highs. Brent crude rose to $109.26 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate closed at $105.42, marking a significant weekly advance driven by tightening global supply expectations and heightened geopolitical risk in key shipping routes. The oil rally came as traders reacted to growing concerns around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passageway for global energy flows. Roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments pass through the corridor, making it a key pressure point for markets whenever tensions escalate. Energy stocks broadly benefited from the move. Chevron and ConocoPhillips both posted solid gains, while the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund also advanced even as broader equity markets weakened Exxon Mobil closed Friday at $157.92, up 3.4% for the session, marking its strongest weekly performance in recent months. The stock rose consistently throughout the May 11–15 trading week, supported by rising crude prices and increased investor appetite for energy exposure. Trading activity was also elevated, with nearly 27.9 million shares exchanged on Friday alone, making it the most active session of the week. The stock moved higher from $149.68 at the start of the week, reflecting steady momentum across the energy sector. Analysts noted that while Exxon’s upstream business benefits directly from higher crude prices, other factors such as refining margins, hedging strategies, and taxation can still influence how closely earnings track oil movements. A key catalyst behind Friday’s rally was the resolution of a long-standing legal case. A Texas jury ruled in Exxon’s favor, clearing the company of liability in a lawsuit dating back to 2016. The case involved investor claims that Exxon allegedly misrepresented reserve valuations tied to Canadian oil sands and Rocky Mountain gas assets. The verdict removes a notable legal overhang that had weighed on sentiment for years. Investors had been monitoring the case closely, as it represented both financial and reputational risk for the energy giant. With the ruling now settled, market attention is shifting away from litigation concerns and back toward fundamentals, particularly oil price trends and production performance. Beyond earnings and oil prices, Exxon now faces a governance spotlight ahead of its upcoming annual meeting scheduled for May 27. Shareholders will vote on a proposal to redomicile the company from New Jersey to Texas, a move management argues reflects its operational base. However, the proposal has faced resistance from major proxy advisory groups, which argue the shift could reduce shareholder oversight of corporate governance decisions. The debate is expected to add volatility around the vote date as institutional investors weigh competing arguments. At the same time, Exxon continues to emphasize its financial strength, having reported $4.2 billion in quarterly earnings and distributed $9.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. CEO Darren Woods has reiterated that the company remains resilient across market cycles and geopolitical disruptions. Heading into Monday’s trading session, Exxon finds itself supported by three key factors: strong crude oil prices, the removal of a major legal risk, and steady operational performance. However, analysts caution that volatility remains possible if oil prices reverse or geopolitical tensions ease. Higher bond yields and shifting inflation expectations could also influence energy sector sentiment, even if crude prices remain elevated. For now, Exxon enters the new week with strong momentum and renewed investor focus, positioning it as one of the most closely watched names in the energy sector. title: Is Exxon Mobil's Recent Surge Sustainable Amid Middle East Tensions? - Kavout
content: Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock has been a standout performer in recent weeks, with shares trading at $154.19 as of March 2, 2026, up 1.11% on the day and nearing its 52-week high of $159.35. This impressive run, which saw the stock climb from $115.15 on November 30, 2025, to $152.50 by March 1, 2026—a 32.4% increase—is largely attributed to a dramatic shift in the global energy landscape. The "Midnight Hammer" crisis in the Middle East, characterized by retaliatory strikes and a de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has injected a significant risk premium into crude oil markets. This geopolitical shock has sent oil prices soaring, with WTI crude currently at $71.15 per barrel, having recently spiked towards $73 and Brent crude briefly touching $100 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for 20% of global seaborne oil, has seen shipping halted and war risk coverage cancelled by marine insurers, effectively stranding an estimated 15 million barrels per day (bpd) of global supply. This immediate supply disruption, combined with a perceived failure of OPEC+ to adequately increase production, has fueled a rapid "risk-off" rotation into hard assets like oil. The market's reaction on March 2, 2026, saw XOM and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) both climb 2.1% by midday, even as the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite tumbled. This divergence underscores a fundamental reassessment of value in an uncertain geopolitical climate, where the "old economy" energy trade has become a defensive hedge. While the immediate catalyst is conflict, the underlying "AI Power Crunch"—the insatiable demand for energy to fuel massive data centers—is also contributing to a structural revaluation of energy companies. However, the sustainability of this surge hinges precariously on the resolution of the Strait of Hormuz standoff. Analysts warn that a diplomatic "off-ramp" within the next 72 hours could lead to a significant cooling of oil prices. Conversely, if the blockade persists, a "super-spike" toward $120 per barrel is possible, which would almost certainly tip the broader global economy into a recession by Q3 2026. This delicate balance means XOM's recent gains, while substantial, are tied to highly unpredictable global events. The current surge in oil prices provides a significant tailwind for Exxon Mobil's Q1 2026 earnings, potentially rewriting near-term cash flow math. Higher crude prices directly enhance the profitability of Exxon's Upstream segment, which saw a 41% increase in revenue in Q1 2025, including a remarkable 234% jump in its U.S. Upstream operations. This segment is particularly sensitive to commodity price fluctuations, making the current environment highly favorable for top-line growth and margin expansion. Despite a 6% decline in net profit and a 15% fall in EPS in Q1 2025 due to weaker refining margins and petrochemicals, the company demonstrated resilience later in the year. Exxon Mobil reported strong Q3 2025 earnings of $7.5 billion and $14.8 billion in cash flow, followed by a Q4 2025 EPS of $1.71, beating estimates. This consistent outperformance, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of earnings beats, suggests an underlying operational strength that can capitalize on improved market conditions. Analysts are already adjusting their expectations, with Bank of America raising ExxonMobil's price target from $135 to $151, reflecting confidence in enhanced future profitability due to the oil risk premium. The consensus Q1 2026 EPS is projected at approximately $1.53, a figure that could prove conservative if oil prices remain elevated throughout the quarter. Exxon's ability to generate substantial free cash flow, projected at $52 billion for the 2025-2026 period, further strengthens its financial position to navigate market dynamics. However, it's not a clear-cut picture. While Upstream benefits, the Energy Products (refining) and Chemical Products segments can face margin pressures. In Q1 2025, Energy Products revenue declined 4% and Chemical Products revenue fell 8%, largely due to falling refining margins and an oversupply in the global chemical market. Therefore, while high crude prices boost one side of the business, investors must monitor product solutions segment margins and overall production guidance during the Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in late April, to gauge the full impact. Beyond the immediate tailwinds from geopolitical tensions, Exxon Mobil's long-term investment thesis is underpinned by its strategic focus on "advantaged barrels" and robust production growth from key assets. The company's operations in Guyana, particularly the Stabroek block, are a cornerstone of this strategy. Projects like Uaru, expected to start up by year-end 2026 with a capacity of 250,000 b/d, and Whiptail, forecast to add another 250,000 b/d next year, are set to boost Guyana's daily oil production well beyond 1 million b/d. Exxon Mobil is also actively developing Guyana's significant recoverable gas resources, especially in the southeast part of the Stabroek block. The Hammerhead project, for instance, is designed to transport gas by pipeline to shore, complementing oil production. The company has already completed its first gas-to-energy pipeline, awaiting an onshore power plant to lower electricity costs in Guyana. This integrated approach to resource development highlights Exxon's commitment to maximizing value from its world-class geology and competitive development costs. The Permian Basin in the U.S. shale patch remains another critical growth engine. CEO Darren Woods has stated there is "no near-term peak Permian" for Exxon, citing over 40 technologies currently in testing to enhance recovery and efficiency. This focus on low-cost, high-margin production in both Guyana and the Permian has made XOM a "HALO" stock (Heavy-Asset, Low Obsolescence) for investors seeking stability and long-term value. Furthermore, Exxon Mobil's commitment to shareholder returns is a significant draw. The company has a strong track record of distributing capital through dividends and share repurchases, having distributed $9.4 billion in Q3 2025 and $9.5 billion in Q4 2025. As a dividend Aristocrat, boasting 26 consecutive annual dividend increases, XOM offers a compelling proposition for income-focused investors, signaling management's confidence in its ability to generate sustained free cash flow and maintain financial discipline. While Exxon Mobil benefits from current market dynamics, several significant risks could derail its long-term investment thesis. The most immediate concern remains commodity price volatility. Despite recent spikes, energy prices are inherently sensitive to geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, and global demand fluctuations. A sharp decline in prices, whether due to de-escalation in the Middle East, falling global demand, or oversupply, could significantly reduce ExxonMobil’s income, particularly in its highly profitable Upstream segment. Beyond oil prices, the company faces regulatory and political risks. Stricter environmental legislation globally, including potential bans on exploration in sensitive regions, new emissions standards, and tighter regulation of refining, could increase operating costs or limit production capacity. The accelerating global energy transition to lower-carbon sources poses a fundamental threat to long-term demand for fossil fuels, potentially diminishing Exxon Mobil's core product revenue streams and creating significant market risks. Exxon Mobil's diversified earnings are also susceptible to global chemical market oversupply and weak refining margins. As seen in Q1 2025, the chemical segment experienced substantial earnings reductions due to "bottom-of-cycle" margins. This cyclicality can act as a significant drag, even when other segments perform well. The capital-intensive nature of its upstream and downstream mix constrains revenue growth assumptions, keeping them modest at around 2.3%. Finally, valuation concerns persist among some analysts. With a TTM P/E ratio of 23.15 and a current price of $154.19, some models suggest the stock is trading at a premium. Analyst consensus price targets range around $140-$142, implying a modest downside from current levels. For instance, one model projects a $140.92 fair value, representing a 6% downside. While the company's beta of 0.35 reflects lower volatility than the broader market, a retreat in oil prices after tensions ease could expose valuation risks, making the stock less attractive at current levels. Navigating the current volatile energy market with Exxon Mobil requires a nuanced approach, balancing short-term tactical plays with long-term strategic considerations. For investors looking to capitalize on immediate geopolitical shocks, XOM's strong correlation with oil prices, coupled with its robust production and cash flow, makes it a compelling option. The stock's beta of 0.35 indicates lower volatility compared to the broader market, offering a degree of stability even in turbulent times. However, a purely short-term strategy is fraught with risk. The unpredictable nature of geopolitical events means any sudden de-escalation could lead to a sharp correction in oil prices and, consequently, in XOM's stock. Investors should consider XOM as a "HALO" stock, benefiting from heavy assets and low obsolescence, but remain vigilant. Monitoring key events like OPEC+ ministerial meetings for changes in production quotas, and geopolitical developments in critical regions like Guyana, is paramount. For long-term investors, Exxon Mobil's status as a dividend Aristocrat, with a current dividend yield of 2.6% and 26 consecutive annual increases, offers a compelling income component. This consistent return to shareholders, alongside disciplined capital allocation and share repurchase programs, provides a defensive moat against market fluctuations. The company's strategic investments in low-cost, high-return assets like the Permian and Guyana further solidify its long-term growth potential, irrespective of short-term price swings. To mitigate risks, diversification remains key. While XOM offers exposure to the energy sector, considering alternatives like ConocoPhillips (COP) for a more pure-play upstream focus, or Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ) for its strong inventory and capital discipline, could balance a portfolio. Ultimately, investors should maintain a conservative position sizing, perhaps 1% to 3% of their portfolio, given the stock's near-term volatility and the cyclical headwinds in its downstream and chemical segments. Exxon Mobil stands at a pivotal juncture, poised to benefit from current geopolitical tailwinds while navigating inherent industry volatility. Its strategic asset base and commitment to shareholder returns offer a compelling long-term narrative, but investors must remain acutely aware of the risks. title: 1 Brilliant Energy Stock to Buy Now and Hold for the Long Term - The Globe and Mail
content: Integrated energy companies have businesses that span the entire energy value chain. Giants like Chevron and ExxonMobil are great options for most investors looking at the energy sector. I own TotalEnergies, which is repositioning its business today for a cleaner future. The geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has Wall Street excited about oil stocks. Given the supply constraints that the conflict has created, pushing energy prices sharply higher, that makes complete sense. But the truth is that this event isn't really all that unusual. The energy sector has a long history of being volatile. That's why most investors should focus on financially strong integrated energy giants. U.S.-based Chevron(NYSE: CVX) and ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM) are good choices, as they have both demonstrated their ability to survive the entire energy cycle. However, I've chosen to buy the French integrated giant TotalEnergies(NYSE: TTE). Here's why you may want to buy it, too. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » The energy sector is inherently volatile. Investors are excited by today's high oil prices, pushing stocks across the industry higher. However, oil and natural gas are commodities, so they rise and fall over time. Eventually, the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East will end. At that point, the supply constraints that led to higher commodity prices will ease, and commodity prices will likely fall. This might take a while to play out, but history is very clear about what to expect over the long term. Most investors should tread with caution when buying energy stocks. The industry is actually broken into three parts: the upstream (energy production), the midstream (pipelines), and the downstream (chemicals and refining). The upstream and the midstream are commodity-driven and volatile, often performing differently through the energy cycle. The midstream is fee-based, so it tends to be a more consistent cash flow generator. If you want to lean into oil prices, you should buy a U.S.-based upstream company like Devon Energy(NYSE: DVN) or Diamondback Energy(NASDAQ: FANG). But if you are a more conservative investor, stick with integrated giants and their diversified businesses. Having exposure to the entire energy value chain helps to smooth out financial performance over time. Exxon and Chevron are great examples, noting that both have rewarded investors with decades of annual dividend increases. They also have the strongest balance sheets in their peer group, with debt-to-equity ratios of 0.2x and 0.25x, respectively. (European competitors tend to carry more debt and more cash on their balance sheets.) Chevron's 3.8% dividend yield gives it an edge over Exxon's 2.7%. TotalEnergies is also an integrated energy giant. Its yield is 4.6%, but U.S. investors have to pay French taxes and fees on that, some of which can be claimed back at tax time. So yield alone isn't the reason why I prefer TotalEnergies. It also has higher leverage, which is the norm for the European competitors. The important difference is clean energy. Exxon and Chevron have chosen to stick pretty close to their core, only dipping their toes into the clean energy sector. TotalEnergies is making a more concerted effort to expand its clean energy portfolio. In 2025, the company's integrated power division, which is where its clean energy investments live, accounted for nearly 12% of its business. Essentially, TotalEnergies is using profits from its carbon fuel operations to build a substantial clean energy business. I believe this is a brilliant decision that aligns TotalEnergies with the world's actual energy demand dynamics. This is the same reason why I own Enbridge(NYSE: ENB), a Canadian midstream company that is also building a clean energy business. I'm happy that TotalEnergies just reported strong earnings, largely thanks to its trading division's ability to capitalize on volatile energy prices. But I have my eye on the long-term shifts taking place in the energy sector, because eventually oil markets will stabilize and investors will move on to a different high-profile trade. Oil and natural gas will remain important energy sources for decades to come. Investors should have exposure to the sector, with integrated energy giants likely to be the best option for most. Exxon and Chevron are both solid choices for more conservative investors. However, the shift toward cleaner energy sources is the big long-term trend. Investors shouldn't ignore it. TotalEnergies allows you to invest in an integrated energy giant while, at the same time, hedging your bets with clean energy. For me, that's the best long-term solution in the energy patch. title: Will SpaceX Spend Its IPO Billions on Real Estate? - The Globe and Mail
content: As SpaceX prepares to IPO, rumors about the company are flying. The latest rumor: SpaceX is buying land to build a second Starbase in Louisiana. When an initial public offering (IPO) is in the offing, it can create a lot of wild rumors -- some of which might even be true. Take the case of SpaceX. As the world's biggest rocket company, and Elon Musk's vehicle for IPO'ing xAI and reIPO'ing Twitter, prepares to become the largest IPO in history, a new rumor has emerged on the internet: Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Continue » Elon Musk is buying up swampland in Louisiana to build a second Starbase spaceport. Does this sound odd? And yet it might actually be true. In a post on X earlier this week, realtor Jim Keaty of Keaty Real Estate (tagline: "Louisiana's most innovative real estate team") is cited as claiming that "SpaceX may have acquired or is acquiring 136k acres (212 sq miles) of marshland" on the Louisiana coast. SPACEX: A realtor named Jim Keaty of Keaty Real Estate published a rumor of possible SpaceX land acquisition in Louisiana. It states SpaceX may have acquired or is acquiring 136k acres (212 sq miles) of marshland south of Highway 82 toward the Gulf of America in Pecan Island... https://t.co/3mv5Do8sTPpic.twitter.com/c36x41kNMw The post goes on to point out that the land parcel in question: It's that last bit that might be of most interest to investors. As far as the general rumor goes, SpaceX came halfway to confirming it in an official X post on Tuesday, conceding that it is "constantly exploring to find viable sites to expand Starship operations in the future, both domestically and internationally." It's no secret that we intend to launch Starship a lot, targeting thousands of flights per year. That cadence will require the ability to launch from many different locations, so we are constantly exploring to find viable sites to expand Starship operations in the future, both... https://t.co/6TrcaGrvVe But consider, too, the implications of the poster's observation about Cheniere Energy(NYSE: LNG) and Golden Pass LNG -- a liquefied natural gas terminal in which ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM) holds a 30% interest, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Although the SpaceX Starship rocket is still conducting flight tests and has not yet been certified to fly national security missions, for example, recent flight tests have proven increasingly successful, providing evidence that Starship is on the right path to beginning commercial operations. Once it does, Elon Musk is on record predicting the spacecraft will eventually reach a launch cadence of 24 per day worldwide, flying "both domestically and internationally." And here's the thing: Musk is going to need a lot of (natural) gas to make all those trips. Each Starship launch is estimated to consume approximately 1,040 metric tons of methane rocket fuel (methalox), which is produced by purifying and cooling natural gas. Or put more simply: Liquefied natural gas is rocket fuel. It makes sense that, when seeking new launch sites, SpaceX would prioritize locations such as Louisiana that have ready access to abundant LNG supplies. The way I read it, this rumor is therefore more likely true than false -- and Cheniere and ExxonMobil may have just found a new favorite customer in SpaceX.
